headline.main: Muhammad Yunus on the Future of Bangladesh: "Politics Is Not My Cup of Tea"
headline.social: Muhammad Yunus on the Future of Bangladesh: "Politics Is Not My Cup of Tea"

intro: Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus became famous through his revolutionary ideas in development aid. For the last half a year, however, he has been head of the interim government in Bangladesh. DER SPIEGEL spoke with him about his frustrations and his hopes for the younger generation.
text:
Muhammad Yunus, 84, walks into the Jamuna State Guest House, a white colonial building with chandeliers and marble floors in the Bangladeshi capital of Dhaka. Though his aides are wearing suits and uniforms, Yunus is wearing a plaid kurta along with a gray vest and trainers. He raises his hand from afar in greeting. "Hello," he calls out, and waves like a schoolboy.
Last summer, demonstrators in Bangladesh overthrew the country's authoritarian prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. The protests were led by university students, many of them not much older than 20 years old. At a time when democracy is facing challenges around the world, Bangladesh, with its population of 174 million people, is seen as a beacon. In August, Yunus was named head of the transition government by the country's president. The economist is widely recognized as the founder of microcredits. His financial institution, Grameen Bank, provides tiny loans to people who had no access to banks. The idea has helped millions of people in poverty. In 2006, the "banker to the poor" received the Nobel Peace Prize.
Bangladesh's prime minister saw Yunus as her archenemy and began refusing to even say his name, instead referring to him as the "bloodsucker of the poor." Yunus says that at times there have been up to 200 active court cases against him. Some of those accusations have since been dropped.
DER SPIEGEL: During your last interview with DER SPIEGEL almost a year and a half ago, you were afraid you were about to be sent to prison. Now you're in the place of the woman who had been hoping to lock you up.
Yunus: Not a bad plot twist, is it?
DER SPIEGEL: You didn't want to go into politics, but now you are head of the interim government. Why the change of heart?
Yunus: The students asked me to. When Hasina's regime fell, I was in a hospital in Paris for a minor operation. I received a call from one of the protest leaders asking me to form the new government. No, no, I said. I can lead organizations, but not a government. But he insisted. I asked for a day to think it over and ultimately decided: The young people have sacrificed their blood, their lives. What I can give is some of the time I have left.
DER SPIEGEL: You then returned to Dhaka?
Yunus: I thought it would take some time before it became official. But two hours later, a nurse brought me flowers and said: "Your Excellency, you are the prime minister of Bangladesh." The news was already out in the press. The doctors discharged me from the hospital early, and the next morning, the French army escorted me to the airport. After arriving in Dhaka, I had to deliver an address to the nation, calling for unity and calm.
DER SPIEGEL: More than half a year has passed since then. How do you view the future of your country?
Yunus: Bangladesh is very fortunate. To the south, it borders the sea and to the north, the Himalayas. This allows us to generate potentially unlimited hydropower. So, energy is not a problem. We are one of the most populous and youngest countries in the world. The average age is 27. Young people are particularly creative, and we are fortunate to have many of them.
DER SPIEGEL: But the protests began because of a quota in the public sector, which many considered unjust. There is a lack of good jobs for young people.
Yunus: And that's why I say: Invest in Bangladesh – especially now. Support the country on its path to democracy. Help the youth. Also for your own sake. Germany is aging and needs workers. Why don't you locate your companies here? The business remains yours, and the profits too. If you create the jobs here, people will stay at home. Otherwise, they'll cross the ocean and knock on your door as immigrants – which upsets so many in the West. Machines, vehicles: Our youth will build them. Forty years ago, we knew nothing about the garment industry. Today, Bangladesh is the second-largest textile exporter in the world. The women from rural areas who work the sewing machines are the most skilled. No one can beat them. Come to Bangladesh!
DER SPIEGEL: You are known as an incorrigible optimist. But the country is suffering from almost double-digit inflation, climate change is already hitting Bangladesh hard, and the police are overstretched.
Yunus: The media likes to focus on the negative. I see opportunities.
DER SPIEGEL: Yet after taking office, you said you found "complete chaos." The prime minister and her party, the Awami League, ruled Bangladesh for 16 years. How did Hasina's system work?
Yunus: Hasina controlled everything. Anyone who didn't play along was punished. It was a regime of fear. We found about 800 torture cells. Horrible places, I went to see them. Critics, activists and human rights lawyers were held without sunlight, like caves, and tortured in electric chairs. To this day, more than 300 people are missing. Government officials and family members enriched themselves for over a decade. In one case, the board of a bank was forced to resign at gunpoint and the government then replaced them with its own people, who extended loans to friends, who knew full well they would never have to repay the money. Since 2009, they pulled an average of $16 billion out of the country every year, totaling around $234 billion.
DER SPIEGEL: It was mainly students who demonstrated on the streets. Initially, they weren’t demanding the prime minister's resignation. But when the police and armed supporters of Hasina began attacking them, their anger turn against the government and the repression. What does your interim government hope to achieve?
Yunus: We are going to hold free elections between December of this year and March of next year. In the meantime, we need to keep the society intact.
DER SPIEGEL: Hasina and her party also came to power after free elections, back in 2009. You have set up 15 reform commissions to prevent the next government from once again undermining the state. They are focusing on changes to the judiciary, to electoral, to police administration and more. How many of the ideas have been implemented so far?
Yunus: The first proposals have come in and we have transferred them into an Excel spreadsheet. We will send this to the political parties and ask for feedback. For each proposal, there are three options: agree, disagree, or agree with requested changes. We will combine the proposals that everyone agrees on into a single document. This document, which everyone will have to sign, will become our July Charter, named after the month of the uprising.
DER SPIEGEL: Like most of your approximately two dozen cabinet members, you don’t belong to a political party. Will the charter legally binding?
Yunus: No, we’re holding the parties to their honor. We are forcing them to make a public commitment. Should we switch from a first-past-the-post system to proportional representation? Should a prime minister's term be limited to two terms, instead of allowing them to remain in power indefinitely, as is currently the case? We will publish the answers on a website so people can see who keeps their word – and who truly wants a new Bangladesh.
DER SPIEGEL: The party that currently appears to have the best chance at winning the next election also has a history of corruption and violence. Do you seriously think anyone will stick to this piece of paper?
Yunus: The parties were surprised when I asked for their opinions. Our interim government has no mandate because we are not elected. We are trying to initiate as many reforms as possible, but only an elected government can implement major changes. And this is the best way we've come up with to get them to do it. The parties will find excuses and delay changes.
DER SPIEGEL: Have you been disillusioned by your time in office?
Yunus: No, I've known that for a long time. In politics, words are often meaningless. They slip away like fish and yet seem clean. Take Hasina: We have evidence of her crimes, yet she sits in exile in India and claims that Yunus wants to establish a Taliban regime in Bangladesh and that he was sent by the Americans. Absurd.
DER SPIEGEL: Ninety percent of Bangladeshis are Muslim, and the country has seen extremist attacks in the past. In 2016, for example, five terrorists stormed a café and killed mainly non-Muslims and foreigners. Some are afraid that Islamist forces could gain influence in the current political vacuum. Is that a concern you share?
Yunus: I am relieved at how liberal our young people are. They fought for the rule of law and religious freedom. Our country could have become very conservative – like Pakistan, from which we seceded in 1971 – but instead, a secular society has emerged. The previous government claimed they were the only ones who could keep Islamism in check. They said everything would fall apart as soon as they left. But that's not true. Nobody here wants an Islamic republic.
DER SPIEGEL: Women's football matches have been cancelled in recent weeks following protests, Sufi shrines have been vandalized, and the Hindu minority is afraid. Doesn't that worry you?
Yunus: Yes, but two years ago, similar incidents also happened, they just weren't reported back then. Today, we have a free press, and that's why we're talking about it.
DER SPIEGEL: The 2011 Arab Spring was a moment of democratic hope, similar to the movement that resulted in the overthrow of Hasina. Back then, though, hope was quickly followed by disappointment in many cases. The old guard proved too strong, and they were frequently more cunning than the revolutionaries. Is Bangladesh at risk of a similar relapse?
Yunus: Unlike during the Arab Spring, the protests here were led by young people who didn't belong to any political party. Now, with an election coming up in a few months, they've realized they can't escape politics. That's why the students founded a party. The youth dream of a new Bangladesh – of democracy, freedom and the right to express their own opinions. They are ready to protect what they have shed their blood for. A team from the UN Human Rights Office visited Bangladesh after the uprising and found evidence of crimes against humanity. Hasina ordered security forces and armed supporters to shoot at the demonstrators. 1,400 people are dead, including teenagers and children. People watched as their friends and family members died in the streets. The new generation is extraordinary.
DER SPIEGEL: Recently, people from that same young generation used an excavator to demolish Hasina's father's house, who proclaimed Bangladeshi independence from that very house in 1971. How can the country move forward when many have revenge on their minds?
Yunus: Hasina incited it. She addressed the people from exile. Many didn't know what to do with their anger.
DER SPIEGEL: There were other cases of arson and violence.
Yunus: I condemn these actions. We, as the interim government, stand for law and order. I tell the people: Trust in the law – and reach out to one another. We need reconciliation.
DER SPIEGEL: Seven weeks ago, the U.S. government abolished the development agency USAID, though the courts have since blocked elements of that order. What impact has this had on Bangladesh?
Yunus: For now, we're managing because we're not heavily dependent on USAID funds. However, we have taken in 1.2 million Rohingya refugees from Myanmar and the end of USAID is hitting them particularly hard. The World Food Program had to cut their food rations by half. The Americans have promised to exempt the Rohingya from the cuts, but whether that will happen remains to be seen. Fortunately, others, like the EU, have announced they will step in.
DER SPIEGEL: Many democrats around the world are worried about U.S. President Donald Trump. Do you share their concern?
Yunus: I wouldn't put it that way. We're about to sign an agreement with billionaire Elon Musk and his satellite internet service Starlink and I have spoken with Musk on the phone. He knows my work and me and says he's an admirer. That's good, because in this way, we have direct contact with someone in the inner circle.
DER SPIEGEL: You have often criticised development aid because of the dependencies you believe it creates. Do you welcome the decision on USAID in some ways?
Yunus: If I could speak to Trump, I would tell him: Don't stop development aid, but don’t give the money to charities. Invest it in social business instead.
DER SPIEGEL: That is your concept of social entrepreneurship, which does not aim to make a profit, seeking instead to solve social problems using economic principles. Companies, for example, sell solar cells to poor people and reinvest the profits.
Yunus: Trump is a businessman. We are businessmen. I'm sure the idea would make sense to him.
DER SPIEGEL: You became known for revolutionizing development aid in the 1980s when you questioned traditional charity with microcredit. Are there parallels between your previous and current work?
Yunus: In my old life, I was a kind of one-man show and could make my own decisions. Now I have to consult political bodies. In the past, my ideas were implemented directly. Today, they may end up on some desk somewhere and it takes time for things to happen.
DER SPIEGEL: You're saying that now that you're in power, you can't make things move?
Yunus: That's right. Politics is not my cup of tea. I can't work like that.
DER SPIEGEL: Are you looking forward to your time as head of the interim government being over in a few months?
Yunus: Yes, definitely.
